## Why This Is Asked
Tests precise bit-level reasoning across 128-bit boundaries without loops or conditionals. Evaluates clean use of bitwise operations across data word boundaries and edge-case handling.

## Key Concepts
- 128-bit composition as two 64-bit halves
- Bitwise AND for intersection detection
- Bitwise OR to combine half-results
- Zero-check inference for disjointness

## Code Example
```c
int isDisjoint128(uint64_t hi1, uint64_t lo1, uint64_t hi2, uint64_t lo2) {
  uint64_t m = (hi1 & hi2) | (lo1 & lo2);
  return (m == 0) ? 1 : 0;
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you extend this to 256-bit masks?
- What's the performance impact on different architectures?

## Why This Is Asked

Tests the ability to implement a deterministic, branchless byte-level permutation on a 128-bit value, a common pattern in low-level data encoding and hash-like transformations.

## Key Concepts

- Byte slicing and reassembly
- Unrolled, fixed permutations
- Inlining and branchless bit-twiddling

## Code Example

```c
// P is a 16-element permutation of {0..15}, evaluated at compile time
uint128 permuteBytes128(uint128 x) {
  return ( (x >> (8*0)) & 0xFF) << (8*P[0]) |
         ( (x >> (8*1)) & 0xFF) << (8*P[1]) |
         ...
         ( (x >> (8*15)) & 0xFF) << (8*P[15]);
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you validate the permutation with generic tests without codegen changes?
- How would you adapt to a runtime-permutation while preserving inlining performance?

## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to apply simple bit-tricks succinctly and reason about edge cases without loops. It also shows understanding of bitwise adjacency relationships across 64 bits.

## Key Concepts

- Bitwise AND and right shift
- Detecting pattern overlap without branching
- Constant-time evaluation on fixed width integers

## Code Example

```javascript
function hasConsecutiveOnes(n) {
  // n treated as a 64-bit value; bitwise ops apply to 32-bit in JS
  return (n & (n >>> 1)) !== 0;
}
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Constant-time 128-bit comparison is core in cryptography and DB internals to avoid timing channels; probe understanding of lexicographic, boundary handling without branches.

## Key Concepts
- Branchless logic with masks
- Lexicographic 128-bit comparison
- Handling hi/lo boundaries in constant time

## Code Example
```javascript
typedef struct { uint64_t hi; uint64_t lo; } uint128;
static inline int8_t cmp128(uint128 a, uint128 b) {
  int hi = (a.hi > b.hi) - (a.hi < b.hi); // -1,0,1
  int lo = (a.lo > b.lo) - (a.lo < b.lo);
  int m = -(int)(hi != 0); // -1 when hi != 0, else 0
  return (int8_t)((hi & m) | (lo & ~m));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt this to return a sign-agnostic 0/1/2 encoding for a hash comparison?
- Could you prove this runs in constant time regardless of inputs and compiler optimizations?
